Sulphur-crested cockatoo chicks hatch after a 27-day incubation period (27 days) [ab = 27 days] when eggs are maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a thermal regime that closely matches the typical brood patch temperature of incubating adults. At the moment of hatching, the altricial nestlings possess an initial wet weight of approximately 28 grams [Ww0 = approximately 28 grams], a modest mass that reflects the considerable yolk reserves allocated during embryonic development. This neonatal body mass is notably low relative to the ultimate adult dimensions the bird will eventually attain, representing merely a few percent of the final body weight. The newly hatched chick is completely dependent on parental provisioning, with both parents participating in feeding and brooding duties during the critical first weeks of life. The brevity of the incubation period, combined with the small hatchling mass, aligns with the reproductive strategy observed in many large-bodied psittacines.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active growth in this species (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the departure from the nest, or fledging, occurs approximately 70 days after hatching [tx = approximately 70 days after hatching], a relatively extended period compared to smaller parrot species that reflects the substantial physical investment required to achieve flight-capable wing musculature and fully developed contour feathers. During this nestling phase, the chick undergoes a dramatic transformation from a downy, nearly helpless neonate into a fully feathered juvenile capable of short flights. Parental provisioning continues for several weeks post-fledging, as the young bird refines its foraging skills and develops the muscular coordination necessary for sustained flight. This temporal milestone represents a critical transition point in the life history of this large, long-lived species.

Sexual maturity in the Sulphur-crested cockatoo is reached at approximately 210 days after hatching [tp = approximately 210 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], though captive observations indicate that behavioral and physiological readiness for reproduction often lags behind gonadal maturation. This relatively rapid onset of puberty, achieved within the first year of life, is somewhat surprising given the species' considerable ultimate body size and extended lifespan. However, the onset of gonad maturation does not immediately translate into successful breeding, as social dynamics, territory acquisition, and pair bonding typically introduce additional delays. In wild populations, first-year birds frequently exhibit exploratory courtship behaviors without producing viable clutches, suggesting that ecological constraints rather than physiological limitations dictate the timing of first reproduction. The period to gonadal maturation therefore represents a minimum developmental benchmark rather than a guaranteed timeline for reproductive activity in natural settings.

The first successful breeding event for a Sulphur-crested cockatoo typically occurs 3.5 years after hatching [tR = 3.5 years after hatching] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a delay that reflects the time required to establish a stable pair bond, secure a suitable nesting hollow, and accumulate sufficient body condition for the demands of egg production and chick rearing. Females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with each clutch containing 3 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 3 eggs]. This modest reproductive output is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy, where high parental investment per offspring and low annual fecundity are traded against an extended lifespan. The maximum longevity recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 73 years [am = approximately 73 years] under typical thermal conditions of 40.2 °C, placing it among the longest-lived of all at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]parrot species. Such an extended lifespan allows for repeated breeding attempts over many decades, compensating for the low annual reproductive rate.

The substantial adult body mass, particularly in males, supports the powerful bill musculature required for cracking hard seeds and nuts, a dietary specialization that shapes much of the species' foraging ecology and habitat preferences across its Australian and New Guinean range.
